claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in HEA multilayer coatings is governed by coherency-stress-driven back-stress hardening at A/B compositional interfaces.
Coherency-stress-driven back stresses impede dislocation climb during creep.
Coherency-stress-driven back stresses impede dislocation glide during creep.
Interfacial back-stress hardening lowers the steady-state creep rate relative to a monolithic HEA coating of the same average composition.
Coherency stresses at A/B layer interfaces generate back-stress hardening.
Under load, dislocations accumulate at coherent A/B interfaces.
The stresses associated with coherent interfaces and accumulated dislocations oppose further dislocation climb and glide.
The proposed interfacial mechanism raises the effective activation energy for creep.
The proposed interfacial mechanism lowers the steady-state creep rate.
Multilayer HEA coatings will have steady-state creep rates 20–60% lower than monolithic HEA coatings under the same conditions.
Multilayer HEA coatings will exhibit a higher stress exponent than monolithic HEA coatings under the same conditions.
The proposed mechanism is applicable to coherent multilayers with individual layer thicknesses of 20–100 nm.
The proposed mechanism is applicable at temperatures of 0.4–0.7 Tm.
The proposed mechanism is applicable at applied stresses of 0.2–0.8 GPa.
Outside the specified thickness, temperature, or stress ranges, other mechanisms such as diffusional creep may dominate.
Annealing the multilayer coatings will relieve interface coherency stresses.
